> all defense mechanisms that would preserve data integrity have been determined to be inapplicable

I'm not sure we need this in the requirement; it feels like something to be in the section text. It also raises a philosophical question: how to measure - is there an alternative to sanitization or not? With that, I think we enter the application logic area here, and we should not dictate the functionality for the application. I think just asking security to make a decision for each sanitization use case should do the job.

Here was the target "functional data-field" that comes from the user, that can (and must) be analyzed and documented. But there can also be technical needs that need to keep things safe "deep in the flow" or "deep in the program code". > Anyone have said that sanitization is not a security control? Just stop this (inventing random statements like someone has stated the fact X and then you come and oppose it). Otherwise there is another issue full of noise, demagogy, invented "facts" etc.

I think this is conflating _governance_ with _security control effectiveness_.

HTML sanitization is itself a security control. A mature sanitizer such as DOMPurify, used correctly, can provide strong security value even without a separately published business policy defining every rule in advance.

A documented policy may help consistency and maintenance, but it is not required for sanitization to function as a valid security control.

HTML sanitization is itself a security control. And "used correctly" does not mean configuration, it just needs to be used in client code where frameworks do not have sanitization built-in like Angular.

A documented policy may help consistency and maintenance, but it is not required for sanitization to function as a valid security control.

Now if you want to set a "business policy" that HTML Sanitizers like DOMPurify needs to be used on the client, I would back that.
It is meant to be general.

The current section text for sanitization (it is debated separately, it will be updated, and for everyone - please do not duplicate this discussion here):

> The ideal protection against using untrusted content in an unsafe context is to use context-specific encoding or escaping, which maintains the same semantic meaning of the unsafe content but renders it safe for use in that particular context, as discussed in more detail in the previous section.

> Where this is not possible, sanitization becomes necessary, removing potentially dangerous characters or content. In some cases, this may change the semantic meaning of the input, but for security reasons, there may be no alternative.

So, here is kind of requirement written into the section text - "that if nothing else is allowed, you can use sanitization."

> Adding sanitization to the same list with encoding and call it "transformation" is fundamental mistake that I recommend you to analyze and reconsider the concept. Sanitization modifies the data, and modification is not a transformation.
 
"**modification is not a transformation**" has no basis in any technical standard. Encoding modifies data it changes its binary representation completely. Compression modifies data it reduces its size. By your own definition both would be modifications, not transformations. The distinction you are drawing does not exist every transformation involves modification, and the two terms are not mutually exclusive. 

FYI, In real-world pipelines (Spark, dbt, Airflow, Glue, etc.), sanitization is clearly part of data transformation and I would consider that modification **IS** a form of transformation.

**Encoding** — modifies data from one format to another = modification + transformation
**Compression** — modifies data by reducing size = modification + transformation
**Sanitization** — modifies data by removing harmful content = modification + transformation
**Whitespace trimming** — modifies data by removing characters = modification + transformation

By the way the important part is not modification is part of transformation or not, the important part "**single bit change**" shall we consider integrity violation or trustworthy failure or not in application behavior at every layer?, I will improve my knowledge on terms you are suggesting, if required. **but I believe the main question is still unanswered.**

> fundamental mistake that I recommend you to analyze and reconsider the concept.

I would request reading the comments in their broader context rather than focusing on individual terminology.


# So Far summary for others

For the record, the JSON normalization, datetime conversion, and whitespace trimming examples were not addressed, and the proposed requirement is still pending feedback:
"**Verify that data transformation decisions including sanitization, encoding, and format conversion are documented as intentional architectural decisions.**"

The distinction you are drawing does not exist every transformation involves modification, and the two terms are not mutually exclusive. 

FYI, In real-world pipelines (Spark, dbt, Airflow, Glue, etc.), sanitization is clearly part of data transformation and I would consider that modification **IS** a form of transformation.

**Encoding** — modifies data from one format to another = modification + transformation
**Compression** — modifies data by reducing size = modification + transformation
**Sanitization** — modifies data by removing harmful content = modification + transformation
**Whitespace trimming** — modifies data by removing characters = modification + transformation
